questions.question: What is the difference between a Docker image and a Docker container?
questions.title: Docker Image vs Container — Key Difference
questions.direct_answer: A Docker image is a read-only blueprint containing your application code, dependencies, and runtime — like a class definition in Java. A Docker container is a running instance of that image — like an object instantiated from a class. You can run multiple containers from the same image, each isolated from the others.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Docker's fundamental building blocks and the relationship between static artifacts and runtime instances
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking images and containers are the same thing, or believing you modify an image when you change a running container
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Draw the class-object parallel clearly and mention that containers have their own writable layer on top of the read-only image layers

sections.title: Images as Blueprints, Containers as Running Instances
sections.content:
Think of a **Docker image** as a Java class definition stored in a .class file — it's a read-only template with everything your application needs: the compiled JAR, the JDK runtime, library dependencies, environment variables, and startup commands. When you write a Dockerfile and run docker build, you create this blueprint and store it on your machine.

A **Docker container** is like an object instantiated from that class — when you run docker run, Docker takes the image blueprint and creates a live, isolated process with its own filesystem, network, and memory space. The powerful part: you can launch ten containers from the same Spring Boot image, each running independently on different ports, serving different users, with different runtime data — just like creating ten Customer objects from one Customer class. The image stays unchanged on disk while containers come and go.

sections.title: Key Ideas at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Docker Image|~Read-only blueprint|like a Java class|built by docker build|immutable layers
blue|Docker Container|~Running instance|like an object|started by docker run|writable layer on top
emerald|One to Many|~Many from one image|each isolated|own port and state|image never changes
violet|Persistence|~Containers are ephemeral|writes lost on rm|use volumes|rebuild image for changes

sections.title: One Image, Many Containers (Class vs Object)
sections.content:
```bash
# Image = blueprint (class). Container = running instance (object).
docker build -t order-service:1.0 .            # create the image once

docker run -d --name order-1 order-service:1.0 # instance 1 from the image
docker run -d --name order-2 order-service:1.0 # instance 2 from the SAME image

docker images    # one image (the class)
docker ps        # two containers (the objects)

docker rm -f order-1   # remove an instance — the image stays, ready to run
```

sections.title: When to Build Images vs Run Containers
sections.content: Build a new **Docker image** when you change application code, update dependencies in pom.xml, or modify the Dockerfile itself — this is your CI/CD build step that produces a versioned artifact like myapp:1.2.3. Run a new **container** when you want to deploy that image to a server, test it locally, scale horizontally by adding more instances, or restart after a crash. In a typical Spring Boot workflow: you build the image once on your laptop or in Jenkins, push it to a registry like Docker Hub or AWS ECR, then run multiple containers from that same image across dev, staging, and production environments. Each environment gets identical code because they share the same image, but different configurations through environment variables or mounted files.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Treating containers as mutable**: Freshers often exec into a running container, manually install packages or edit configuration files, then expect those changes to persist. When the container restarts, all manual changes vanish because the image layers are read-only — only the thin writable layer is temporary. The fix: rebuild the image with those changes in the Dockerfile.
- **Confusing image tags with container names**: Running docker run myapp:latest twice creates two separate containers, each with a random name like eloquent_tesla and zen_knuth, both from the same myapp:latest image. Freshers sometimes think the second run replaces the first, but Docker keeps both containers unless you explicitly remove them.
- **Not understanding the writable layer**: When your Spring Boot app writes logs to /var/log inside the container, that data lives in the container's writable layer and disappears on removal — this is why production apps mount volumes for persistent data.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Docker image**: immutable, read-only template built from a Dockerfile containing application code, dependencies, and runtime — analogous to a Java class definition
**Docker container**: running instance of an image with its own isolated process, filesystem, and network — analogous to an object instantiated from a class
**One image, many containers**: you can run unlimited containers from the same image, each on a different port, with different environment variables or volumes
**Writable layer**: containers add a thin writable layer on top of read-only image layers, but changes in this layer are lost when the container is removed
**Immutability**: modifying files inside a running container doesn't change the underlying image — those edits disappear on restart unless you rebuild the image or use volumes
**Registry storage**: images are stored in registries like Docker Hub or private registries, then pulled to machines where you run containers from them
**Lifecycle independence**: deleting a container doesn't delete the image it came from — the image remains available for launching new containers

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: So the key difference is that a Docker image is like a class definition in Java — it's a read-only blueprint that contains your Spring Boot JAR, the JDK, all your dependencies, and the instructions to start your app. When you run docker build, you're creating this template and storing it on your machine. A Docker container is the running instance of that image, kind of like an object you create from a class. When you do docker run, Docker takes that blueprint and spins up an actual process with its own memory, network, and filesystem. Here's the powerful part: you can launch ten containers from the same image, each running on a different port, serving different users, completely isolated from each other — just like creating ten Order objects from one Order class. The image itself never changes when containers are running. One mistake freshers make is thinking that if they exec into a container and manually change a config file, that change is permanent. It's not — the image layers are read-only, and the container just has a thin writable layer on top that gets wiped when you remove the container. If you want permanent changes, you rebuild the image with a new Dockerfile. So remember: image equals blueprint, container equals running copy of that blueprint. You build images once, store them in registries, then run containers from them across all your environments.

groups.heading: Docker image
groups.text: A read-only blueprint. It's built from a Dockerfile, stored on disk as stacked layers, and never modified after creation. Think of it as a Java class definition.

groups.heading: Docker container
groups.text: A running instance created from an image. It has an active process, a writable layer on top of the image, and its own network. Think of it as an object instantiated from that class.

beats.text: You push images to registries and version them. You run containers in your environments. Deploying a new version means building a new image and replacing the running containers — you never patch a live container.

speakable_v2.cap: non-obvious: containers are ephemeral by default. Any files written inside a container disappear when the container is removed. If you need persistence, that's what Docker volumes are for.

questions.question: What do 'docker ps' and 'docker images' show and how are they different?
questions.title: docker ps vs docker images — What They Show
questions.direct_answer: The docker images command lists all Docker images stored on your local machine — these are the blueprints. The docker ps command lists currently running containers — these are the live instances. Use docker ps -a to see all containers including stopped ones. They're different because images are static templates while containers are active processes.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic Docker CLI proficiency and understanding of the image-container distinction in practice
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing the two commands or not knowing that docker ps only shows running containers by default
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Walk through the key columns in docker ps output: CONTAINER ID for reference, IMAGE showing which blueprint was used, STATUS showing container state, and PORTS showing network mappings

sections.title: Inspecting Images vs Inspecting Running Processes
sections.content:
These two commands show you different parts of Docker's lifecycle. **docker images** lists all the blueprints you've downloaded or built on your local machine — these are the read-only templates sitting in your Docker storage at /var/lib/docker. You'll see columns like REPOSITORY (the image name), TAG (the version), IMAGE ID (a unique hash), CREATED (when it was built), and SIZE (how much disk space it uses).

This is like looking at all the JAR files in your Maven local repository. **docker ps** lists actively running containers right now — these are live processes consuming CPU and memory. By default it shows only running containers, so if you start a container, let it run, then stop it, docker ps won't show it anymore unless you add the -a flag to see all containers regardless of state. Think of docker ps as the equivalent of jps or ps aux filtered to Java processes, while docker images is like ls on your lib directory.

sections.title: Key Ideas at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|docker images|~Local blueprints|REPOSITORY and TAG|IMAGE ID and SIZE|templates on disk
blue|docker ps|~Running containers|CONTAINER ID and IMAGE|STATUS and PORTS|live processes only
emerald|docker ps -a|~Include stopped|exited containers|see exit codes|key for debugging
violet|Don't Confuse|~ID columns differ|CONTAINER ID is unique|IMAGE is the source|stopped still on disk

sections.title: Reading docker images vs docker ps Output
sections.content:
```bash
# docker images -> the read-only blueprints stored on disk
docker images
# REPOSITORY        TAG     IMAGE ID       SIZE
# order-service     1.0     a1b2c3d4e5f6   210MB

# docker ps -> containers running RIGHT NOW
docker ps
# CONTAINER ID   IMAGE              STATUS        PORTS
# 9f8e7d6c5b4a   order-service:1.0  Up 3 minutes  0.0.0.0:8080->8080/tcp

# docker ps -a -> include stopped/exited containers (key for debugging)
docker ps -a
# 1a2b3c4d5e6f   order-service:1.0  Exited (1) 2 minutes ago
```

sections.title: docker images vs docker ps Command Output
When to Use Each Command
sections.content:
Run **docker images** when you want to see what blueprints are available locally before running a container, check if you need to pull a new version from a registry, verify that your latest build created the expected image tag, or clean up disk space by identifying large or unused images to delete with docker rmi. Run **docker ps** when you want to check if your Spring Boot container is actually running after you started it, find the container ID to exec into it for debugging, see which port mappings are active so you know where to curl your API, check container status to diagnose why a service isn't responding, or verify that a container restart policy is working after a crash.

Use **docker ps -a** when you need to find a stopped container to restart it, inspect logs from a container that exited with an error, or clean up old containers that are cluttering your system with docker rm.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not using -a flag**: Freshers run docker ps, see no output, and think Docker isn't working — but their container started and immediately exited with an error. Running docker ps -a reveals the stopped container with STATUS showing Exited (1) 2 minutes ago, and docker logs shows the stack trace.
- **Confusing IMAGE ID in docker ps**: The IMAGE column in docker ps output shows the image name or ID the container was created from, not a unique container identifier — that's the CONTAINER ID column. Multiple containers can show the same IMAGE value because they're all instances of the same blueprint.
- **Forgetting containers persist after stopping**: Stopping a container with docker stop doesn't delete it. The container still exists in a stopped state (visible with docker ps -a), consuming disk space. Freshers often run docker run repeatedly, creating dozens of stopped containers without realizing it, until docker ps -a shows a huge list. The fix is docker rm or using the --rm flag on docker run to auto-delete on exit.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **docker images**: lists all Docker image templates stored locally, showing REPOSITORY name, TAG version, IMAGE ID hash, creation date, and storage SIZE
**docker ps**: lists currently running containers only by default, showing CONTAINER ID, IMAGE source, STATUS, and PORTS mappings
**docker ps -a**: includes all containers regardless of state — running, stopped, exited, or paused — essential for debugging and cleanup
**CONTAINER ID vs IMAGE ID**: CONTAINER ID is a unique identifier for a running or stopped container instance, IMAGE ID identifies the blueprint template that container was created from
**STATUS column**: in docker ps output shows container state like Up 3 hours for running, Exited (0) 5 minutes ago for stopped, or Restarting for crash loops
**PORTS column**: displays port mappings like 0.0.0.0:8080->8080/tcp meaning host port 8080 forwards to container port 8080, critical for accessing services
**Ephemeral nature**: stopped containers remain on disk until explicitly removed with docker rm — docker ps -a helps identify these zombie containers for cleanup

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: So docker images and docker ps show you two completely different things. When you run docker images, you're looking at all the blueprints stored on your local machine — the image templates you've either built yourself or pulled from a registry like Docker Hub. You'll see columns like REPOSITORY, which is the image name, TAG for the version, and SIZE showing how much disk space it takes. It's like looking at a list of JAR files sitting in your Maven local repository. On the other hand, docker ps shows you the containers that are actually running right now. These are live processes using CPU and memory. You'll see CONTAINER ID, which is a unique identifier for that running instance, IMAGE showing which blueprint it came from, STATUS like Up 2 hours, and PORTS showing network mappings like host port 8080 forwarding to container port 8080. Here's a key thing freshers miss: docker ps only shows running containers by default. If you start a Spring Boot container and it crashes immediately, docker ps shows nothing. You need docker ps -a to see all containers including stopped or exited ones. That -a flag is critical for debugging because it reveals containers that failed to start. So remember: docker images for blueprints on disk, docker ps for live processes, docker ps -a to see everything including the dead ones.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app packaged as a Docker image
speakable_v2.hook: Two of the most-used Docker commands show completely different things — and mixing them up tells an interviewer you haven't actually used Docker.

groups.heading: docker images
groups.text: Lists all images on your local machine — the read-only blueprints. Shows repository name, tag, image ID, creation date, and size. Images stay until you remove them with docker rmi.

groups.heading: docker ps
groups.text: Lists currently running containers. Shows container ID, which image it came from, the running command, uptime, status, exposed ports, and name. Stopped containers don't appear here.

items: docker ps: running containers only — add -a to see stopped containers too
docker images: all local images regardless of whether any containers are running
You can have an image with zero running containers, and that's normal

beats.text: After you run docker-compose down, docker ps shows nothing. But docker images still shows all your images — they're on disk, ready to run again.

speakable_v2.cap: sharp edge: docker ps -a reveals stopped containers that are consuming disk space. Run docker system prune to clean up stopped containers, dangling images, and unused networks in one go.

questions.question: What is the sequence of steps from pulling a Docker image to running a container?
questions.title: Docker Pull to Running Container — The Full Sequence
questions.direct_answer: First, docker pull downloads an image from a registry like Docker Hub to your local machine — this step is optional because docker run does it automatically if the image isn't found locally. Then docker run creates a new container from that image, sets up networking and volumes, and starts the container process. The full workflow is: pull image from registry, create container instance, start container process.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Docker's basic workflow and the relationship between registries, local images, and running containers — foundational knowledge for deployment
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not realizing that docker run automatically pulls missing images, or thinking docker pull is always required before running a container
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that docker run is actually a convenience command that combines docker create which sets up the container without starting it and docker start which launches the process — understanding this split helps with debugging and advanced workflows

sections.title: From Registry to Running Process in Three Steps
sections.content:
The journey from an image sitting in a remote registry to a running container on your machine happens in three logical steps. **Step 1: Pull the image** — docker pull fetches an image from a registry like Docker Hub, AWS ECR, or a private registry, downloads all its layers, and stores them in your local Docker storage at /var/lib/docker. This is like downloading a JAR from Maven Central to your local .m2 repository. **Step 2: Create the container** — docker create (or the create phase inside docker run) takes the local image and sets up a container instance: it allocates a unique container ID, prepares the filesystem by stacking the image's read-only layers plus a new writable layer on top, configures network interfaces, and mounts any specified volumes. At this point the container exists but isn't running yet — it's like having a JVM process ready but not yet started. **Step 3: Start the container** — docker start (or the start phase inside docker run) launches the container's main process as specified in the image's CMD or ENTRYPOINT, connects standard I/O streams, and hands control to the application. Now your Spring Boot app's main method executes and the service is live.

In practice, you rarely use docker pull explicitly because docker run handles it automatically if the image isn't local.

sections.title: Key Ideas at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|1. Pull|~Fetch from registry|docker pull image|downloads layers|optional step
blue|2. Create|~Set up the container|alloc ID and filesystem|network and volumes|not running yet
emerald|3. Start|~Launch the process|runs the ENTRYPOINT|app goes live|Spring Boot boots
violet|docker run|~All three at once|pull if missing|create plus start|-d for detached

sections.title: Manual Step-by-Step vs Automatic docker run
When to Use Each Step Separately
sections.content:
Use **docker pull explicitly** when you want to pre-download images on production servers before deploying, avoiding download delays during container startup — this is common in CI/CD pipelines where you pull images in a separate stage then run them later. Also pull ahead of time to verify that a specific image tag exists in the registry and fail fast if it's missing.

Use **docker create without starting** when you need to inspect or modify the container configuration before running it, attach additional volumes or networks that weren't specified initially, or prepare multiple containers that will start simultaneously with docker start (useful for orchestrated startup sequences).

Use **docker run with -d detached mode** for typical production deployments where you want a single command that handles pull, create, and start atomically, with the container running in the background.

Use **docker run without -d interactive mode** for debugging, running one-off commands like database migrations, or executing shell sessions where you need to see output directly and interact with the process.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Assuming docker pull is mandatory**: Freshers write deployment scripts with docker pull followed by docker run, not realizing docker run already pulls missing images automatically. The extra pull command wastes time when the image is already local and adds unnecessary complexity to scripts.
- **Not understanding the create-start split**: Running docker run, seeing the container ID printed, then running docker run again with the same --name, which fails with a name conflict error because the first run already created a container with that name. The container exists but might have exited immediately due to an error — use docker ps -a to see it and docker start to restart it instead of creating a duplicate.
- **Forgetting -d flag in production**: Running docker run without -d in a deployment script, which blocks the terminal and makes the container exit when the SSH session closes or the script terminates. Production containers should always run detached with -d unless you're deliberately running an interactive shell or short-lived command.
- **Ignoring pull failures**: A docker run command silently tries to pull an image with tag latest, fails because the registry is unreachable or authentication is missing, then Docker falls back to a stale local cache of that tag, running outdated code without the fresher noticing the pull failure in the logs.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **docker pull**: downloads an image from a registry like Docker Hub or AWS ECR to local storage, fetching all layers and storing them in /var/lib/docker
**docker create**: sets up a container instance from a local image — allocates container ID, prepares filesystem layers, configures network and volumes — but doesn't start the process
**docker start**: launches the main process in an existing container, executing the CMD or ENTRYPOINT defined in the image
**docker run**: convenience command that combines pull (if image is missing locally), create, and start into a single atomic operation
**Automatic pull**: docker run checks if the specified image tag exists locally, and if not, automatically pulls it from the registry before creating the container
**Detached mode**: -d flag runs the container in the background, returning control to the terminal — essential for production deployments
**Interactive mode**: running docker run without -d keeps the container attached to your terminal, useful for debugging or running one-off commands like shell sessions

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The sequence from pulling an image to running a container has three steps, but in practice you usually do it with one command. First is docker pull, which downloads the image from a registry like Docker Hub to your local machine. Docker fetches all the layers that make up that image and stores them in your local Docker storage. This is optional because docker run does it automatically if the image isn't already local. Second is docker create, which takes that local image and sets up a container instance. Docker allocates a unique container ID, stacks the read-only image layers with a new writable layer on top, configures network interfaces, and mounts any volumes you specified. At this point the container exists but it's not running yet — nothing is actually executing. Third is docker start, which launches the container's main process. For a Spring Boot app, this is where your application's main method gets called and the server starts listening on its port. Now here's the thing: you almost never run these commands separately. The docker run command does all three steps automatically — it pulls the image if it's missing, creates the container, and starts it in one shot. You can add -d to run it in detached mode so it goes to the background, which is what you want in production. The reason it's useful to know about the three-step split is for debugging. If a container keeps failing to start, you can use docker create to set it up without starting it, inspect the configuration, maybe attach extra volumes or change the command, then manually docker start it. But for normal deployments, docker run does everything you need.

speakable_v2.hook: Most people jump straight to docker run — but knowing what actually happens under the hood shows you understand Docker, not just its commands.

items: docker pull: fetches the image from a registry to your local cache
docker run: creates a container from the image and starts it immediately
If the image isn't local, docker run pulls it automatically first
Internally, docker run = docker create + docker start in one step

beats.text: When you first run docker run eclipse-temurin:21 on a fresh machine, Docker checks local cache, finds nothing, pulls the image layers from Docker Hub, then starts the container. Next time it uses the cached image and starts in seconds.

Stopping and cleanup: docker stop sends SIGTERM to the main process for graceful shutdown. After a timeout it sends SIGKILL. Docker rm removes the stopped container. Docker rmi removes the image from local storage.

speakable_v2.cap: candidates miss: a stopped container still exists and takes up disk space. Use docker ps -a to see it, and docker system prune to clean up all stopped containers at once.

questions.question: What are Docker image layers and how does layer caching work?
questions.title: Docker Image Layers and Layer Caching
questions.direct_answer: Docker images are built from layers — each instruction in your Dockerfile like RUN, COPY, or ADD creates a new read-only layer. Docker caches these layers by content hash, so if a layer hasn't changed since the last build, Docker reuses the cached version instead of rebuilding it. This makes subsequent builds much faster.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of how Docker builds work and whether you've optimized real Dockerfiles for faster iteration
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing Dockerfiles that copy all source code first, then install dependencies — this invalidates the cache on every code change and forces a full rebuild
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the optimization pattern: copy dependency files first like pom.xml or build.gradle, run dependency download, then copy source code — so the expensive dependency layer stays cached even when code changes

sections.title: Layers as Incremental Filesystem Changes
sections.content:
Every line in your Dockerfile that modifies the filesystem creates a new **layer** — think of layers as transparent sheets stacked on top of each other, where each sheet captures one set of changes. When you write FROM openjdk:17, that pulls a base image with multiple layers (the OS, the JDK installation).

Then RUN apt-get install curl adds a new layer containing the curl binary. COPY target/app.jar /app.jar adds another layer with your JAR file. Docker assigns each layer a unique **hash** based on the instruction and its inputs — if the instruction and context haven't changed, the hash stays the same. During docker build, Docker checks its local cache: if a layer hash matches one from a previous build, Docker skips executing that instruction and reuses the cached layer, saving minutes on dependency downloads or compilation. This is huge for Spring Boot builds where downloading Maven dependencies can take 3-5 minutes but happens only once if you structure the Dockerfile right.

sections.title: Key Ideas at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Layer|~One Dockerfile step|RUN, COPY, ADD|read-only|content-hashed
blue|Cache Hit|~Unchanged is reused|skips the step|saves minutes|deps not re-downloaded
emerald|Invalidation|~Flows downward|a change breaks the rest|stable on top|volatile at bottom
violet|Java Pattern|~Split the COPY|pom.xml first, go-offline|src copy later|fast rebuilds

sections.title: Optimized Dockerfile with Layer Caching for Spring Boot
sections.content:
FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jre
WORKDIR /app

# Copy only dependency descriptor first
COPY pom.xml ./
COPY .mvn ./.mvn
COPY mvnw ./

# Download dependencies - this layer is cached until pom.xml changes
RUN ./mvnw dependency:go-offline

# Now copy source code - changes here don't invalidate dependency layer
COPY src ./src

# Build the JAR - only reruns when src or pom.xml changes
RUN ./mvnw package -DskipTests

# Final layer: define startup command
CMD ["java", "-jar", "target/order-service-1.0.0.jar"]

sections.title: When Layer Caching Matters Most
sections.content:
Layer caching is critical during **local development iteration** when you're changing Java code frequently but dependencies stay stable — proper layer ordering cuts rebuild time from 5 minutes to 30 seconds. It's also essential in **CI/CD pipelines** where every commit triggers a Docker build: if your Dockerfile copies source code before installing dependencies, every code change forces a full Maven or Gradle dependency download, wasting build minutes and slowing deployments.

Use multi-stage builds with layer caching when you **compile inside Docker** — copy pom.xml first, download dependencies in one layer, then copy source in a later layer so the expensive download is cached. For **production images**, layer caching during build reduces registry push time because unchanged layers don't need to be uploaded again, only the layers with new code. If you're working with a **monorepo** where multiple services share dependencies, cache the shared dependency layer so all service images benefit.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Copying everything first**: The classic mistake is COPY . . at the top of the Dockerfile before installing dependencies. Every time you change a single Java file, Docker sees the source directory hash changed and invalidates the cache from that point forward, forcing a complete re-download of Maven dependencies even though pom.xml hasn't changed. This turns a 30-second rebuild into a 5-minute wait.
- **Using latest tags in FROM**: Writing FROM openjdk:latest seems convenient but breaks caching because Docker can't tell if latest points to a different image than last time — it pulls the image again every build. Pin versions like FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jre-jammy instead.
- **Not understanding cache invalidation scope**: Freshers think changing line 10 only invalidates that layer, but Docker invalidates that layer and all subsequent layers — order matters. If you put COPY src before RUN apt-get install curl, a source code change forces curl to reinstall.
- **Ignoring the build context**: Sending the entire project directory including node_modules, .git, or target folders as build context makes the COPY instruction hash enormous and cache-unfriendly — use a .dockerignore file to exclude irrelevant directories.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Layer**: each Dockerfile instruction that changes the filesystem (RUN, COPY, ADD) creates a new read-only layer with a unique content-based hash
**Cache hit**: if a layer's instruction and inputs haven't changed since the last build, Docker reuses the cached layer instead of re-executing the instruction
**Cache invalidation**: changing a layer invalidates that layer and all subsequent layers in the Dockerfile — earlier layers remain cached
**Optimization pattern**: copy dependency files like pom.xml first, install dependencies, then copy source code — keeps the expensive dependency layer cached across code changes
**Build context**: Docker sends the entire directory (build context) to the daemon — large contexts slow down builds even with caching, so use .dockerignore to exclude unnecessary files
**Multi-stage builds**: combine layer caching with multi-stage Dockerfiles to separate build-time dependencies from runtime, keeping final images small while caching build layers
**Registry efficiency**: when pushing to a registry, only layers that changed are uploaded — unchanged cached layers are skipped, saving bandwidth and time

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Docker images aren't built as one monolithic file — they're actually a stack of layers, where each layer represents the filesystem changes from one Dockerfile instruction. When you write RUN apt-get install curl, that creates a layer containing just the curl binary and its dependencies. When you do COPY target/app.jar, that's another layer with your JAR file. Docker assigns each layer a hash based on the instruction and the files involved. Here's where caching comes in: before executing an instruction, Docker checks if it has a layer with the same hash from a previous build. If it does, Docker skips that instruction entirely and reuses the cached layer, which can save minutes on a Spring Boot build. The trick is instruction order. Freshers often write COPY dot-dot at the top, copying all source code, then RUN mvnw install to download dependencies. That's backwards — every code change invalidates the cache and forces a full dependency re-download. The right way is copy pom.xml first, run dependency download, then copy source code. Now when you change Java code, the dependency layer stays cached because pom.xml didn't change. It's the difference between a 5-minute rebuild and a 30-second rebuild. One gotcha: changing any layer invalidates that layer and everything after it, so put the most stable stuff at the top like base image and dependencies, and the frequently changing stuff like source code near the bottom.

speakable_v2.hook: Every line in your Dockerfile creates a layer — and the order you write those lines determines whether your builds take 10 seconds or 5 minutes.

beats.text: Docker images are built as a stack of layers. Each instruction in a Dockerfile — FROM, COPY, RUN — adds one immutable layer on top of the previous ones. The final image is all those layers combined.

Layer caching is the real payoff. If a layer's instruction and its inputs haven't changed since the last build, Docker reuses the cached version instead of rebuilding it. One changed layer invalidates all layers below it.

For Java, the optimization is to COPY pom.xml first and run Maven dependency download as a separate layer. That dependencies layer gets cached. Then COPY your source code. Now when you change a Java file, only the compile layer rebuilds — the multi-minute dependency download is skipped.
production trap: copying all source files in a single COPY instruction means any file change invalidates the dependency download layer, making every build slow. Split COPY into two steps.

speakable_v2.cap: Put the things that change least at the top of the Dockerfile, and the things that change most — your source code — at the bottom. Cache invalidation flows downward.

questions.question: What does it mean that Docker containers are ephemeral, and how do you persist data?
questions.title: Docker Containers Are Ephemeral — Persisting Data
questions.direct_answer: Ephemeral means container filesystem changes are lost when the container is removed — any data you write inside the container disappears. To persist data across container restarts or share data between containers, use Docker volumes, which are managed storage areas that exist outside the container lifecycle and survive container deletion.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of container lifecycle and data persistence strategies — critical for production apps with databases, file uploads, or logs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming data written inside a container like uploaded files or database writes is permanent, then losing application state or user data when the container restarts
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish between Docker volumes managed by Docker in /var/lib/docker/volumes and bind mounts direct mapping to a host directory — both persist data but volumes are portable across environments while bind mounts are good for development hot-reloading

sections.title: Containers Are Temporary, Data Needs a Home
sections.content:
**Ephemeral** means containers are designed to be disposable — you can delete one and spin up a fresh replacement without losing functionality, as long as configuration and data live outside the container. When your Spring Boot app writes a log file to /var/log/app.log inside the container, that file lives in the container's **writable layer**, a thin filesystem overlay on top of the read-only image layers.

Stop and remove the container with docker rm, and that writable layer is deleted permanently — your logs vanish. This is by design: containers should be stateless, treating local filesystem writes as temporary scratch space. For data that must survive — database files, user uploads, application logs, configuration that changes at runtime — you use **Docker volumes** or **bind mounts**. A volume is a directory managed by Docker, stored outside the container in /var/lib/docker/volumes on the host. You attach it to a container at a specific mount point like /var/lib/mysql, and all writes to that path go to the volume instead of the writable layer. When you remove the container, the volume persists, and you can attach it to a new container, preserving all the data.

sections.title: Key Ideas at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Ephemeral|~Disposable by design|writes in the writable layer|gone on docker rm|stateless-friendly
blue|Docker Volume|~Managed storage|outside the lifecycle|survives removal|-v data colon path
emerald|Bind Mount|~Host dir mapping|-v host colon container|great for dev|less portable
violet|Rule|~Match the workload|stateless: ephemeral is OK|stateful: use volumes|a DB needs a volume

sections.title: Spring Boot App with Volume for Uploaded Files
When to Use Volumes vs Bind Mounts
sections.content:
Use **Docker volumes** in production for database storage like Postgres data directories, application logs you want to aggregate or rotate externally, user-uploaded files that must persist across deployments, or any state that needs to survive container replacement during rolling updates. Volumes are managed by Docker, portable across hosts, and can be backed up with docker volume commands.

Use **bind mounts** in development when you want hot-reloading — mount your local src/main/java directory into the container so code changes reflect immediately without rebuilding the image. Bind mounts are also useful for injecting configuration files at runtime, like mounting a local application.yml to /app/config/application.yml so you can tweak settings without rebuilding. For **shared data between containers**, use a named volume attached to multiple containers — for example, a logs volume mounted by both your app container and a Fluentd log shipper. For **read-only reference data** like ML models or static assets, use a bind mount with :ro flag to prevent accidental modification.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Writing critical data inside the container**: Freshers deploy a Spring Boot app with an embedded H2 database writing to /data/app.db inside the container, then restart the container to apply a config change — all user data is lost because /data wasn't mounted to a volume. The writable layer is ephemeral by default.
- **Not understanding volume lifecycle**: Creating a container with -v mydata:/app/data, then removing the container with docker rm — the volume mydata still exists on the host, but freshers think it's gone and create a new volume, leading to orphaned volumes consuming disk space. Use docker volume ls and docker volume prune to manage them.
- **Confusing volumes and bind mounts**: Trying to use a bind mount like -v /local/path:/container/path on a production server where /local/path doesn't exist or has different permissions, causing the app to crash. Volumes are more portable because Docker manages the host path.
- **Permission mismatches**: Mounting a host directory with root ownership into a container running as a non-root user — the app can't write to the mount point and fails with permission denied errors. The fix is setting correct ownership with chown in the Dockerfile or using named volumes where Docker handles permissions.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Ephemeral**: container filesystem changes in the writable layer are lost when the container is removed — data written to unmounted paths disappears permanently
**Docker volume**: managed storage area in /var/lib/docker/volumes on the host, persists across container lifecycle, attached with -v volumename:/container/path
**Bind mount**: direct mapping of a host directory to a container path like -v /host/dir:/container/dir, useful for development but less portable than volumes
**Named volumes**: created with docker volume create or automatically when specified in -v, can be shared across multiple containers, managed with docker volume ls and docker volume rm
**Anonymous volumes**: created without a name, identified by hash, harder to manage and reattach, generally avoided in favor of named volumes
**Volume drivers**: Docker supports plugins for remote storage like NFS, AWS EBS, or Ceph, allowing volumes to be backed by cloud storage instead of local disk
**Data persistence strategy**: production apps should mount volumes for databases, logs, uploads, and any state that must survive deployments or crashes

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Ephemeral means containers are designed to be temporary and disposable. When you write data inside a container — like saving a file to /var/log or writing to a local database file — that data lives in the container's writable layer, which is just a thin filesystem overlay on top of the read-only image. The moment you remove the container with docker rm, that writable layer gets deleted and all your data is gone. This is intentional: Docker wants containers to be stateless so you can delete one and spin up a fresh copy without worrying about cleanup. But obviously that's a problem for real apps. If you're running Postgres in a container and the database files are stored inside the container, restarting it wipes all your tables. That's where volumes come in. A Docker volume is storage managed by Docker that exists outside the container lifecycle. You create a volume and attach it to a container at a specific mount point, like -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data. Now when Postgres writes to that directory, the data goes to the volume on the host machine, not the container's writable layer. You can remove the container, create a new one, attach the same volume, and all your data is still there. There's also bind mounts, which are direct mappings from a host directory to a container path. These are great for development — you can mount your source code directory so changes reflect immediately without rebuilding the image. The difference is volumes are managed by Docker and more portable, while bind mounts depend on specific host paths. The mistake freshers make is deploying an app that writes important data inside the container without mounting a volume, then losing everything on the first restart.

speakable_v2.standard_example: MySQL container with a Docker volume for database persistence
speakable_v2.hook: Ephemeral sounds scary but it's actually a feature — until you run a database container without a volume and lose all your data on restart.

beats.text: Every container has a thin writable layer on top of the read-only image. Anything written inside the container — files, logs, database rows — goes into that writable layer. When you remove the container, that layer is deleted. That's what ephemeral means.

For stateless apps like a Spring Boot REST API, this is fine. The app doesn't write anything locally, so ephemeral containers work perfectly. For stateful workloads like a database, you need data to survive container restarts.

items: Docker volume: Docker-managed storage outside the container lifecycle — survives docker rm
Bind mount: maps a specific host directory into the container — useful for dev
Usage: docker run -v mydata:/var/lib/mysql mysql attaches a volume at the database data path

beats.text: gotcha: if you run a MySQL container in local dev without a volume and then run docker-compose down, you lose your entire local database. Always define volumes for stateful services in docker-compose.yml.

speakable_v2.cap: Stateless containers love being ephemeral. Stateful containers need volumes. Knowing the difference is what separates a developer who understands Docker from one who just copies commands.
